source_witnesses.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

children.title: Scaling Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces for coordinate, basis, gradient, or model scaling choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform positive-definiteness contract for variable-metric scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scaling interface at iteration \(k\) accepts the available history and returns a symmetric matrix \(M_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), or its action on vectors, satisfying fixed spectral bounds \(0<\mu\le L<\infty\): \[\mu\lVert v\rVert^2\le v^\top M_kv\le L\lVert v\rVert^2\quad\text{for every }v\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] If the direction is defined by \(d_k=-M_k^{-1}g_k\) for a nonzero gradient or estimator \(g_k\), then the interface must supply a solve or operator application consistent with the same \(M_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Return a symmetric positive-definite scaling operator with uniform eigenvalue bounds and a consistent inverse action.
assumptions_latex: The returned operator is symmetric on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_k\) is uniformly positive definite and \(g_k^\top d_k=-g_k^\top M_k^{-1}g_k<0\) whenever \(g_k\ne0\).

notation.meaning: uniform lower and upper spectral bounds

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Coupled Stepsize-Scaling Calibration
children.top_down_role: Compatibility considerations when stepsize selection depends on the chosen scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Stepsize-Scaling Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint acceptance rule for metric scaling and stepsize selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_k\) and a nonzero first-order vector \(g_k\), generate trial pairs \((M_{k,j},\alpha_{k,j})\) with \(M_{k,j}\) symmetric and \(\mu I\preceq M_{k,j}\preceq LI\), and set \(d_{k,j}=-M_{k,j}^{-1}g_k\). Accept the first pair satisfying \(\alpha_{\min}\le\alpha_{k,j}\le\alpha_{\max}\) and \(f(x_k+\alpha_{k,j}d_{k,j})\le f(x_k)+\sigma\alpha_{k,j}g_k^\top d_{k,j}\), where \(0<\sigma<1\). Return the accepted metric, stepsize, direction, and \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_{k,j}d_{k,j}\); if no pair passes within the trial budget, return failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search jointly over bounded metrics and stepsizes, accepting the first pair satisfying spectral and sufficient-decrease conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every successful pair yields \(g_k^\top d_k<0\) and satisfies the stated sufficient-decrease inequality.

They do not directly establish this coupled search rule, its first-acceptable-pair policy, or its finite-budget failure contract.

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Search Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Armijo backtracking restricted to a computed sketch subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a differentiable objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), an iterate \(x_k\), an orthonormal basis \(Q_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\), and a reduced direction \(p_k\in\mathbb{R}^r\) satisfying \(\nabla f(x_k)^{\mathsf T}Q_kp_k<0\), initialize \(\alpha=\bar\alpha>0\). While \(f(x_k+\alpha Q_kp_k)>f(x_k)+c\alpha\nabla f(x_k)^{\mathsf T}Q_kp_k\), replace \(\alpha\) by \(\beta\alpha\), where \(c,\beta\in(0,1)\). Return the accepted stepsize \(\alpha_k=\alpha\) and update \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kQ_kp_k\). The interface reports the accepted scale and the number of objective evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backtracking scales a descent direction lying in the sketch subspace until the Armijo sufficient-decrease inequality holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x_{k+1})\le f(x_k)+c\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k)^{\mathsf T}Q_kp_k

notation.meaning: Orthonormal basis of the current sketched subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Free Subspace Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface contract for selecting reduced steps without user-supplied smoothness or scale constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each iteration \(k\), the interface receives \(x_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), an orthonormal subspace basis \(Q_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r_k}\), the projected gradient \(g_k=Q_k^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(x_k)\), and the history \(\mathcal H_k=\{g_i,p_i,f(x_i):i<k\}\). A parameter-free selector returns \(p_k=\mathcal A(\mathcal H_k,g_k)\in\mathbb{R}^{r_k}\) and the method sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k+Q_kp_k\). The selector may use fixed numerical safeguards but accepts no user-supplied Lipschitz constant, strong-convexity modulus, gradient bound, optimal value, or target accuracy; any scale estimate must be computed from \(\mathcal H_k\) and current oracle data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter-free selector computes each reduced step entirely from observed history and current oracle data, without problem-scale constants supplied by the user.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_k=\mathcal A(\mathcal H_k,Q_k^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(x_k))\ \text{uses no user-supplied problem-scale parameter}

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and interface formulation fit the leaf, but the asserted meaning of parameter-free—including the exact list of excluded inputs and permitted safeguards—is convention-dependent and has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Initial Orthogonalization
children.top_down_role: Orthogonalization choices used when forming or extending a subspace basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Initial Orthogonalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Modified Gram–Schmidt insertion of a new vector into an existing basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(Q=[q_1,\ldots,q_r]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\) with orthonormal columns, a candidate \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and a tolerance \(\tau>0\), set \(w=v\). For \(j=1,\ldots,r\), compute \(h_j=q_j^{\mathsf T}w\) and replace \(w\) by \(w-q_jh_j\). Let \(\rho=\lVert w\rVert_2\). If \(\rho>\tau\lVert v\rVert_2\), return \(q_{r+1}=w/\rho\) and the enlarged basis \([Q,q_{r+1}]\); otherwise declare the candidate numerically dependent and retain \(Q\). This record describes the first orthogonalization pass, before any selective or full reorthogonalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One modified Gram–Schmidt pass removes components along the stored basis, then normalizes or rejects the residual according to a dependence tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho>\tau\lVert v\rVert_2\Rightarrow q_{r+1}=w/\rho;\quad \rho\le\tau\lVert v\rVert_2\Rightarrow v\text{ is rejected}

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits initial orthogonalization, and the one-pass modified Gram–Schmidt procedure is internally coherent. A source is still required for the particular relative rejection rule and its interpretation as numerical dependence.

children.title: Selective Reorthogonalization
children.top_down_role: Targeted reorthogonalization triggered for selected basis vectors or detected degradation.

knowledge_statements.title: Selective Reorthogonalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A second projection pass triggered by an orthogonality-defect test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After an initial orthogonalization produces a nonzero residual \(w\) against an orthonormal basis \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\), compute \(\eta=\lVert Q^{\mathsf T}w\rVert_2/\lVert w\rVert_2\). Given a trigger \(\gamma>0\), perform no further work when \(\eta\le\gamma\). When \(\eta>\gamma\), compute \(c=Q^{\mathsf T}w\), replace \(w\) by \(w-Qc\), and recompute its norm. Accept \(q=w/\lVert w\rVert_2\) only if \(\lVert w\rVert_2>\tau\lVert v\rVert_2\); otherwise report numerical dependence. Thus reorthogonalization is applied only when the measured loss of orthogonality exceeds the prescribed trigger.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second projection pass is performed only when the normalized component of the residual in the stored subspace exceeds a trigger.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \eta>\gamma\Rightarrow w\leftarrow(I-QQ^{\mathsf T})w

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selective-reorthogonalization role is appropriate, but v is used in the acceptance threshold without being introduced in this record. The defect trigger and dependence policy also lack source support, so the reliable corrected formulation depends on a cited algorithmic convention.

children.title: Full Reorthogonalization
children.top_down_role: Comprehensive reorthogonalization of the maintained basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Full Reorthogonalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconditional second modified Gram–Schmidt pass against every retained basis vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an orthonormal basis \(Q=[q_1,\ldots,q_r]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\), a candidate \(v\ne0\), and tolerance \(\tau>0\), set \(w=v\). For each pass \(\ell=1,2\) and each \(j=1,ldots,r\), compute \(h_j^{(\ell)}=q_j^{\mathsf T}w\) and replace \(w\) by \(w-q_jh_j^{(\ell)}\). After both complete passes, accept \(q=w/\lVert w\rVert_2\) if \(\lVert w\rVert_2>\tau\lVert v\rVert_2\); otherwise declare numerical dependence. Unlike selective reorthogonalization, the second pass is executed for every candidate and every retained basis vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every accepted candidate undergoes two complete modified Gram–Schmidt passes before normalization, regardless of its measured orthogonality defect.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lVert w\rVert_2>\tau\lVert v\rVert_2\Rightarrow q=w/\lVert w\rVert_2

notation.meaning: Coefficient removed for basis vector j during pass l.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the loop range contains the malformed token 'ldots' instead of '\ldots'. A source is also required for identifying exactly two unconditional modified Gram–Schmidt passes and the stated rejection threshold as the intended full-reorthogonalization policy.

children.title: Numerical Rank Detection
children.top_down_role: Detection of effective rank within a computed or maintained subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Rank Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative singular-value threshold for the effective rank of a basis or sketch matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\) have singular values \(\sigma_1(B)\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_q(B)\ge0\), where \(q=\min\{n,m\}\). Given an absolute tolerance \(\tau_{\mathrm{abs}}\ge0\) and relative tolerance \(\tau_{\mathrm{rel}}\ge0\), define \(\theta=\max\{\tau_{\mathrm{abs}},\tau_{\mathrm{rel}}\sigma_1(B)\}\). The numerical rank is \(r_\theta(B)=\#\{i:\sigma_i(B)>\theta\}\). Directions associated with singular values at most \(\theta\) are classified as numerically unresolved; this convention makes the detected rank explicitly dependent on the scale and chosen tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Numerical rank counts singular values exceeding the larger of an absolute cutoff and a cutoff relative to the largest singular value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_\theta(B)=\#\{i:\sigma_i(B)>\max(\tau_{\mathrm{abs}},\tau_{\mathrm{rel}}\sigma_1(B))\}

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits numerical rank detection and the formula is internally precise, but the strict singular-value cutoff and max-combination of absolute and relative tolerances are conventions requiring a cited numerical-linear-algebra source.

children.title: Basis Compression
children.top_down_role: Reduction of basis size while retaining selected subspace information.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncated-SVD replacement of a redundant basis matrix by a smaller orthonormal basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\), a target dimension \(r\le\operatorname{rank}(B)\), and a thin singular value decomposition \(B=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\), form \(U_r=[u_1,\ldots,u_r]\), \(\Sigma_r=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r)\), and \(V_r=[v_1,\ldots,v_r]\). Return the compressed orthonormal basis \(Q_c=U_r\) and, when coordinates must be transferred, the map \(T=\Sigma_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\), so that \(Q_cT=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\). The output is the best rank-\(r\) approximation to \(B\) in both spectral and Frobenius norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Truncated SVD replaces a redundant matrix by its leading left singular vectors and supplies a coordinate map for the retained approximation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lVert B-Q_cT\rVert_2=\sigma_{r+1}(B),\qquad Q_c^{\mathsf T}Q_c=I_r

notation.meaning: Map from original columns to compressed coordinates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compression algorithm is standard, but the best-approximation claim requires a source. Moreover, sigma_{r+1}(B) is undefined as written when r=min(n,m); a sourced replacement must state the corresponding zero-residual boundary convention or separate that case.

children.title: Rank-Aware Compression
children.top_down_role: Compression policies guided by detected numerical rank.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Aware Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compression dimension selected from a numerical-rank threshold rather than fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(B=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\) and a cutoff \(\theta\ge0\), set \(r=r_\theta(B)=\#\{i:\sigma_i(B)>\theta\}\). If \(r=0\), return the empty basis and declare that no direction is numerically resolved. Otherwise return \(Q_c=U_{:,1:r}\) and \(T=\Sigma_{1:r,1:r}V_{:,1:r}^{\mathsf T}\). Then \(Q_c\) has orthonormal columns, \(Q_cT\) retains every singular component above the cutoff, and the discarded spectral-norm residual equals \(\sigma_{r+1}(B)\le\theta\), with \(\sigma_{q+1}(B)=0\) when \(r=q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The retained dimension equals the detected numerical rank, so compression discards exactly the singular components at or below the chosen cutoff.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lVert B-Q_cT\rVert_2=\sigma_{r+1}(B)\le\theta

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind matches the leaf and the stated SVD truncation is coherent, including the supplied full-rank convention. The cutoff-based rank selection and residual claim nevertheless need an inspectable numerical-linear-algebra source.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Certificate Checks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computable residual checks for orthogonality, reconstruction, and retained numerical rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a computed compression \(B\approx QT\), with \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\), define \(\delta_{\mathrm{orth}}=\lVert I_r-Q^{\mathsf T}Q\rVert_2\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{rec}}=\lVert B-QT\rVert_2/\max\{1,\lVert B\rVert_2\}\), and \(\delta_{\mathrm{rank}}=\max\{0,\theta-\sigma_r(B)\}\), taking \(\delta_{\mathrm{rank}}=0\) when \(r=0\). Given tolerances \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{orth}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rec}}\ge0\), the tuple \((Q,T,r)\) passes the certificate when \(\delta_{\mathrm{orth}}\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{orth}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{rec}}\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rec}}\), and either \(r=0\) or \(\sigma_r(B)>\theta\). These directly computable inequalities certify numerical orthogonality, reconstruction quality, and consistency of the retained rank with the cutoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The certificate accepts a compressed basis only when orthogonality, reconstruction error, and the singular-value rank cutoff all pass explicit numerical tests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta_{\mathrm{orth}}\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{orth}},\quad \delta_{\mathrm{rec}}\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rec}},\quad r=0\ \text{or}\ \sigma_r(B)>\theta

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the terminal container, but the rank check only verifies sigma_r(B)>theta and does not verify that the first discarded singular value satisfies sigma_{r+1}(B)<=theta. Thus it does not certify that r equals the cutoff-defined numerical rank. The finite-precision thresholds and a corrected two-sided rank check require source support.

children.title: Parallel-Streaming-Distributed Execution Interface
children.top_down_role: Execution interfaces only; full systems analysis belongs to the parallel and distributed chapter.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Independent Sketches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concurrent construction and aggregation of independently randomized reduced spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), let \(S_k^{(1)},\ldots,S_k^{(p)}\) be mutually independent random sketch matrices. Worker \(i\) computes \(Y_k^{(i)}=\Phi_kS_k^{(i)}\), where \(\Phi_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) is the common operator or data matrix, and returns an orthonormal basis \(Q_k^{(i)}=\operatorname{orth}(Y_k^{(i)})\). After all available workers return, form \(Y_k=[Q_k^{(1)},\ldots,Q_k^{(p)}]\) and output \(Q_k=\operatorname{orth}(Y_k)\). Conditional on \(\Phi_k\), sketch generation and local basis construction require no communication; only the returned bases are aggregated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers independently sketch the same operator, orthogonalize locally, and combine their returned bases into one aggregate subspace.
assumptions_latex: S_k^{(1)},\ldots,S_k^{(p)}\text{ are mutually independent conditional on }\Phi_k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{range}(Q_k)=\sum_{i=1}^p\operatorname{range}(\Phi_kS_k^{(i)})

notation.meaning: Independent sketch used by worker i.

source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

source_witnesses.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and range-sum conclusion fit parallel independent sketches, but the cited general architecture section does not specifically support independent randomized sketches, local orthogonalization, or basis aggregation. A sketching-specific source with a precise locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Sketch Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact aggregation of additive linear sketches computed from row-partitioned data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}\) be row-partitioned as \(A=[A_1^{\mathsf T},\ldots,A_p^{\mathsf T}]^{\mathsf T}\), and conformably partition a sketch matrix \(S=[S_1^{\mathsf T},\ldots,S_p^{\mathsf T}]^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times s}\). Worker \(i\) computes the local contribution \(G_i=A_i^{\mathsf T}S_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times s}\). A sum reduction returns \(G=\sum_{i=1}^pG_i\), which equals the centralized sketch \(A^{\mathsf T}S\). Consequently, any basis \(Q=\operatorname{orth}(G)\) obtained after exact aggregation spans the same subspace as centralized construction from the same partitioned sketch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summing compatible worker-local sketch products exactly reproduces the centralized linear sketch and therefore its resulting subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^p A_i^{\mathsf T}S_i=A^{\mathsf T}S

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous Subspace Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic reduced updates computed from boundedly stale iterates and subspace bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a shared iterate be \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). At logical update \(k\), a worker reads a stale copy \(\hat x_k=x_{k-d_k}\) with \(0\le d_k\le D\), constructs an orthonormal basis \(Q_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r_k}\), computes \(g_k=Q_k^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(\hat x_k)\), and forms a reduced step \(p_k=-\alpha_k g_k\) with \(\alpha_k>0\). The worker atomically applies \(x_{k+1}=x_k+Q_kp_k\) without requiring other workers to synchronize. The update record stores \((k,d_k,Q_k,p_k)\), allowing the implementation to reject updates whose measured delay exceeds \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each worker computes a subspace step from a boundedly stale read and atomically adds it to the current shared iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kQ_kQ_k^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(x_{k-d_k})

notation.meaning: Read delay at logical update k.

knowledge_statements.title: Streaming Subspace Maintenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental orthonormal-basis maintenance with fixed rank and optional forgetting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a target rank \(r\), forgetting factor \(\rho\in(0,1]\), and vectors \(a_t\in\mathbb R^d\), initialize an orthonormal matrix \(Q_0\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}\) and \(C_0\succeq0\). At time \(t\), form \(Y_t=[\sqrt{\rho}Q_{t-1}C_{t-1}^{1/2},a_t]\), compute a rank-\(r\) truncated singular value decomposition \(Y_t\approx Q_t\Sigma_tV_t^{\mathsf T}\), and set \(C_t=\Sigma_t^2\). The maintained subspace is \(\mathcal U_t=\operatorname{range}(Q_t)\); after any finite stream, output \(Q_t\) and \(C_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Update a fixed-rank orthonormal basis from each arriving vector by truncating a factorization of the previous weighted summary augmented with the new observation.
assumptions_latex: Each \(a_t\) is available once in streaming order.
A rank-\(r\) truncated singular value decomposition can be computed at each update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_t^{\mathsf T}Q_t=I_r\) and \(\mathcal U_t=\operatorname{range}(Q_t)\) summarizes the dominant rank-\(r\) directions of the exponentially weighted stream.

notation.meaning: maintained orthonormal basis after observation t

review_flags: A precise streaming subspace reference is required for this truncated-factor update and its approximation interpretation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the streaming-maintenance leaf, but no source supports this particular truncated-factor recurrence or the claim that its recursively truncated summary represents the dominant directions of the exponentially weighted stream. A source should also fix the dimension of C_t and the intended treatment of rank-deficient updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Overdetermined Least Squares
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean linear least squares with at least as many equations as unknowns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(m\ge n\), the overdetermined least-squares problem is \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\frac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2.\] Its solution set is \(\{x:A^{\mathsf T}(Ax-b)=0\}\). If \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\), the objective is strongly convex, the solution is unique, and it equals \(x_\star=(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}b\); the residual \(b-Ax_\star\) is orthogonal to \(\operatorname{range}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An overdetermined least-squares problem fits more equations than unknowns; full column rank gives a unique solution characterized by the normal equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimizers satisfy \(A^{\mathsf T}(Ax-b)=0\), and full column rank yields the displayed unique solution.

children.title: Underdetermined Linear Systems
children.top_down_role: Subspace-method interfaces for linear systems with nonunique feasible solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Underdetermined Linear Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistent linear systems having fewer equations than unknowns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m<n\) and let \(b\in\operatorname{range}(A)\). The underdetermined linear system is the feasibility problem \(Ax=b\). For any particular solution \(x_0\), its complete solution set is the affine space \[\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b\}=x_0+\ker(A).\] If \(A\) has full row rank, this space has dimension \(n-m>0\), so the system has infinitely many solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consistent system with fewer equations than unknowns has an affine solution set obtained by adding every null-space vector to one particular solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every solution is uniquely expressible as \(x=x_0+z\) with \(z\in\ker(A)\) once \(x_0\) is fixed.

notation.meaning: null space of the system matrix

children.title: Minimum-Norm Solution Selection
children.top_down_role: Interfaces that target a minimum-norm representative among feasible solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Norm Solution Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moore–Penrose selection for a consistent underdetermined system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank and let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). Among all solutions of \(Ax=b\), there is a unique minimum-Euclidean-norm solution, represented by \[x_\star=A^\dagger b=A^{\mathsf T}(AA^{\mathsf T})^{-1}b.\] It is characterized equivalently by \(Ax_\star=b\) and \(x_\star\in\operatorname{range}(A^{\mathsf T})=\ker(A)^\perp\). For every feasible \(x=x_\star+z\) with \(z\in\ker(A)\), one has \(\lVert x\rVert_2^2=\lVert x_\star\rVert_2^2+\lVert z\rVert_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pseudoinverse chooses the unique feasible vector orthogonal to the null space, and every other solution has strictly larger norm unless identical.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\star=A^\dagger b\) is the unique member of \(\{x:Ax=b\}\) minimizing \(\lVert x\rVert_2\).

children.title: Null-Space Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Effects of unresolved null-space components on subspace selection or returned solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Null-Space Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness of linear-system solutions along invisible null-space directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), suppose \(Ax_0=b\). Then \(A(x_0+z)=b\) for every \(z\in\ker(A)\), and conversely every solution of \(Ax=b\) has this form. Consequently, observations depending only on \(Ax\) cannot distinguish parameters in the same coset \(x_0+\ker(A)\). A solution is unique exactly when \(\ker(A)=\{0\}\); otherwise any selection rule must impose an additional criterion, such as minimum norm or regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear observations cannot distinguish solutions differing by a null-space vector; uniqueness holds exactly when the matrix has a trivial null space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution set equals \(x_0+\ker(A)\), and uniqueness is equivalent to \(\ker(A)=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: affine equivalence class of indistinguishable solutions

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Regression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Penalized linear regression with a proper convex regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(R:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and \(\lambda>0\), regularized regression is \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\;F(x):=\frac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2+\lambda R(x).\] A point \(x_\star\) is optimal exactly when \(0\in A^{\mathsf T}(Ax_\star-b)+\lambda\partial R(x_\star)\). If \(F\) is coercive, a minimizer exists; if \(F\) is strictly convex, that minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularized regression adds a convex penalty to least-squares loss; optimality balances the data gradient against a penalty subgradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimizers are precisely the points satisfying \(0\in A^{\mathsf T}(Ax-b)+\lambda\partial R(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Subspace Gauss–Newton
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauss–Newton iteration restricted to a sampled parameter subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=\tfrac12\lVert r(x)\rVert_2^2\) with differentiable \(r:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), initialize \(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\). At iteration \(k\), sample \(P_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times s}\), compute \[u_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in\mathbb R^s}\frac12\lVert r(x_k)+J(x_k)P_ku\rVert_2^2,\] choose \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) by a prescribed acceptance or line-search rule, and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kP_ku_k\). Stop when the projected gradient norm \(\lVert P_k^{\mathsf T}J(x_k)^{\mathsf T}r(x_k)\rVert_2\) is below tolerance, and output \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample a parameter subspace, solve the Gauss–Newton residual model within it, globalize the step, and stop on a projected-gradient test.
assumptions_latex: \(r\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of the iterates.
Each subproblem has a selected least-squares minimizer.
The sampling and acceptance rules are specified in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every update lies in \(\operatorname{range}(P_k)\) and minimizes the linearized residual model over that sampled subspace before globalization.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the residual map at x

knowledge_statements.title: Sketched Jacobian Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced gradient and Gauss–Newton curvature induced by a parameter-space sketch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\tfrac12\lVert r(x)\rVert_2^2\), let \(J=J(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and let \(P\in\mathbb R^{n\times s}\). Restricting the local displacement to \(p=Pu\) gives the model \[m_P(u)=\frac12\lVert r(x)+JPu\rVert_2^2.\] Its reduced gradient and Gauss–Newton matrix are \(g_P=P^{\mathsf T}J^{\mathsf T}r(x)\) and \(H_P=P^{\mathsf T}J^{\mathsf T}JP=(JP)^{\mathsf T}(JP)\). Thus the products \(JP\) and \(P^{\mathsf T}J^{\mathsf T}r(x)\) contain all Jacobian information required to solve the restricted quadratic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a parameter-subspace step, the sketched Jacobian product determines both the reduced gradient and the reduced Gauss–Newton matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(P\in\mathbb R^{n\times s}\) is fixed for the local model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_P=P^{\mathsf T}J^{\mathsf T}r(x)\) and \(H_P=(JP)^{\mathsf T}(JP)\) completely specify the restricted Gauss–Newton normal equations.

notation.meaning: Jacobian restricted to the sampled parameter subspace

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Model Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of residual-model norms through a subspace embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\) and \(P\in\mathbb R^{n\times s}\), and define \(\mathcal V=\operatorname{span}(\{r(x)\}\cup\operatorname{range}(J(x)P))\). If \(S\in\mathbb R^{q\times m}\) satisfies \((1-\varepsilon)\lVert v\rVert_2^2\le\lVert Sv\rVert_2^2\le(1+\varepsilon)\lVert v\rVert_2^2\) for every \(v\in\mathcal V\), then for every \(u\in\mathbb R^s\), \[(1-\varepsilon)m(u)\le\widetilde m(u)\le(1+\varepsilon)m(u),\] where \(m(u)=\tfrac12\lVert r(x)+J(x)Pu\rVert_2^2\) and \(\widetilde m(u)=\tfrac12\lVert S(r(x)+J(x)Pu)\rVert_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An embedding that preserves the residual and restricted Jacobian span preserves every restricted linearized residual-model value by the same relative factors.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a \((1\pm\varepsilon)\) squared-norm embedding on \(\mathcal V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For all \(u\in\mathbb R^s\), \((1-\varepsilon)m(u)\le\widetilde m(u)\le(1+\varepsilon)m(u)\).

notation.meaning: span of the residual and restricted Jacobian range

review_flags: A dedicated source is required for the residual-model transfer statement under a subspace embedding.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is mathematically coherent: every residual-model vector lies in the stated span, so the assumed squared-norm embedding yields the displayed model-value bounds. No evidence is supplied, however, for this residual-model transfer result in the sketched nonlinear least-squares interface.

children.title: Independent Component Sampling
children.top_down_role: Component selection performed without conditioning on the chosen subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Component Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional independence requirement for finite-sum component selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x)\), let \(\mathcal F_k\) contain all randomness revealed before iteration \(k\). Component sampling is independent of the contemporaneous subspace draw \(P_k\) when an index \(I_k\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\) is drawn according to probabilities \(p_i>0\), independently of \(P_k\) conditional on \(\mathcal F_k\): \[\mathbb P(I_k=i,\,P_k\in B\mid\mathcal F_k)=p_i\,\mathbb P(P_k\in B\mid\mathcal F_k)\] for every index \(i\) and measurable set \(B\). Then \(g_k=\nabla f_{I_k}(x_k)/(Np_{I_k})\) is conditionally unbiased for \(\nabla f(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Draw a finite-sum component independently of the current subspace; inverse-probability weighting then gives an unbiased component-gradient estimator.
assumptions_latex: \(I_k\) and \(P_k\) are conditionally independent given \(\mathcal F_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[g_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)\).
review_flags: A source for conditionally independent component and subspace sampling in finite-sum optimization is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, and inverse-probability weighting is standard. No source is supplied for the conditional component–subspace sampling model, and the unbiasedness conclusion also relies on x_k being measurable with respect to the prior-history sigma-algebra, which is only implicit.

children.title: Independent Subspace Sampling
children.top_down_role: Subspace selection performed without conditioning on the chosen objective component.

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Subspace Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional independence and isotropy requirements for sampled search subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times s}\) be the iteration-\(k\) subspace matrix and let \(\mathcal F_k\) denote the prior history. Independent subspace sampling requires that, conditional on \(\mathcal F_k\), \(P_k\) is independent of the contemporaneous component index \(I_k\). A normalized isotropy condition is \[\mathbb E[P_kP_k^{\mathsf T}\mid\mathcal F_k]=I_n.\] Consequently, for every \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable vector \(v\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\mathbb E[\lVert P_k^{\mathsf T}v\rVert_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\lVert v\rVert_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample the search subspace independently of the current component and normalize it so projected squared norms are unbiased.
assumptions_latex: \(P_k\) and \(I_k\) are conditionally independent given \(\mathcal F_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every prior-measurable \(v\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[\lVert P_k^{\mathsf T}v\rVert_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\lVert v\rVert_2^2\).
review_flags: A source fixing the normalization convention and conditional sampling model is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the independent-subspace leaf, and the projected-norm identity follows from the displayed conditional isotropy assumption. A source is required to establish that this scaling and conditional-independence convention is the intended interface rather than one of several common sketch normalizations.

children.title: Product-Distribution Pairing
children.top_down_role: Joint sampling interfaces formed from separately specified component and subspace distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Distribution Pairing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint law of independently sampled component and subspace variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_k\sim p\) on \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\) and \(P_k\sim\mu\) on a measurable space of subspace matrices. If the draws are conditionally independent given \(\mathcal F_k\), their conditional joint law is the product measure \[\mathcal L((I_k,P_k)\mid\mathcal F_k)=p\otimes\mu.\] Hence, for every integrable measurable \(h\), \[\mathbb E[h(I_k,P_k)\mid\mathcal F_k]=\sum_{i=1}^N p_i\int h(i,P)\,\mu(dP).\] In particular, integrable factors separate: \(\mathbb E[a(I_k)b(P_k)\mid\mathcal F_k]=\mathbb E[a(I_k)\mid\mathcal F_k]\mathbb E[b(P_k)\mid\mathcal F_k]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent component and subspace draws have a product joint distribution, so joint expectations are iterated sums and integrals and separable factors decouple.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) and \(\mu\) are the conditional marginal laws given \(\mathcal F_k\).
\(I_k\) and \(P_k\) are conditionally independent given \(\mathcal F_k\).
The displayed test functions are conditionally integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L((I_k,P_k)\mid\mathcal F_k)=p\otimes\mu\), with the displayed expectation factorization.
review_flags: A source connecting the product-measure formulation to the finite-sum subspace-sampling interface is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the product-distribution leaf, and the factorization is standard when p and mu are conditional probability kernels. No source is supplied, and a dedicated reference should confirm the conditional product-law formulation and clarify that p and mu may depend measurably on the prior history.

children.title: Component-Conditioned Subspace Sampling
children.top_down_role: Subspace selection conditioned on the sampled objective component.

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Conditioned Subspace Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional subspace selection after sampling a finite-sum component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\in[n]\) denote a component index and let \(S\in\mathcal S\) denote a subspace sketch from a finite nonempty family. Component-conditioned subspace sampling is specified by a probability mass function \(\rho\) on \([n]\) and, for every \(i\in[n]\), a probability mass function \(q_i\) on \(\mathcal S\). The joint law is \[\mathbb P(I=i,S=s)=\rho_i q_i(s).\] Whenever \(\rho_i>0\), this gives \(q_i(s)=\mathbb P(S=s\mid I=i)\); for \(\rho_i=0\), the choice of \(q_i\) does not affect the joint law. Thus the sketch distribution may vary with the sampled component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample a component and then draw a subspace from its component-specific probability distribution. Their joint probability is the product of the component probability and that distribution; distributions attached to zero-probability components are immaterial.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb N\) and \(\mathcal S\) is finite and nonempty.
\(\rho_i\ge0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n\rho_i=1\), and each \(q_i\) is a probability mass function on \(\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(I=i,S=s)=\rho_iq_i(s)\).

notation.meaning: component-specific sketch probability, equal to the conditional probability when rho_i is positive

review_flags: Exact component-conditioned formulation lacks a directly matching supplied source locator.

children.title: Subspace-Conditioned Component Sampling

knowledge_statements.title: Subspace-Conditioned Component Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional finite-sum component selection after sampling a subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\in\mathcal S\) denote a subspace sketch from a finite nonempty family and let \(I\in[n]\) denote a component index. Subspace-conditioned component sampling is specified by a probability mass function \(\pi\) on \(\mathcal S\) and, for every \(s\in\mathcal S\), a probability mass function \(r_s\) on \([n]\). The joint law is \[\mathbb P(I=i,S=s)=\pi_s r_s(i).\] Whenever \(\pi_s>0\), this gives \(r_s(i)=\mathbb P(I=i\mid S=s)\); for \(\pi_s=0\), the choice of \(r_s\) does not affect the joint law. Hence the component distribution may depend on the selected subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample a subspace and then select a component from its subspace-specific probability distribution. Their joint probability is the product of the subspace probability and that distribution; distributions attached to zero-probability subspaces are immaterial.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb N\) and \(\mathcal S\) is finite and nonempty.
\(\pi_s\ge0\), \(\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\pi_s=1\), and each \(r_s\) is a probability mass function on \([n]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(I=i,S=s)=\pi_s r_s(i)\).

notation.meaning: subspace-specific component probability, equal to the conditional probability when pi_s is positive

children.title: Joint Component-Subspace Sampling Laws
children.top_down_role: Directly specified joint laws for coordinated component and subspace selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Component-Subspace Sampling Laws
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General coupled law for finite component and subspace indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A joint component-subspace sampling law is a probability mass function \(p:[n]\times\mathcal S\to[0,1]\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}p_{i,s}=1\). It determines marginals \(p_i=\sum_s p_{i,s}\) and \(p_s=\sum_i p_{i,s}\). Whenever the relevant marginal is positive, its conditional factorizations are \[p_{i,s}=p_i\,p(s\mid i)=p_s\,p(i\mid s).\] Independence is the special case \(p_{i,s}=p_i p_s\); otherwise the component and subspace choices are coupled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A joint probability table describes all coupled component-subspace draws and factors in either conditional direction; factorization into its marginals characterizes independence.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb N\) and \(\mathcal S\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{i,s}=p_i p(s\mid i)=p_s p(i\mid s)\) on positive-marginal events.

notation.meaning: joint probability of component i and sketch s

review_flags: Probability identities are standard, but no supplied locator directly treats coupled component-subspace laws.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite joint-law, conditional-factorization, and independence statements are mathematically standard and fit the definition container, but no source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Sketched Estimator Storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compressed storage of projected component-gradient surrogates in fixed sketch bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For component functions \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), fix matrices \(U_i\in\mathbb R^{d\times r_i}\) with orthonormal columns and reference points \(\alpha_i\). Store only \(y_i=U_i^{\mathsf T}\nabla f_i(\alpha_i)\in\mathbb R^{r_i}\). The corresponding ambient-space surrogate is recovered as \[h_i=U_i y_i=U_iU_i^{\mathsf T}\nabla f_i(\alpha_i).\] The table therefore stores \(\sum_{i=1}^n r_i\) scalars, rather than \(nd\), while representing each projected component estimator exactly. It does not retain gradient components orthogonal to \(\operatorname{range}(U_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Store coordinates of each component gradient in a fixed low-dimensional sketch basis; multiplying by that basis exactly reconstructs the projected, but not the full, gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_i=U_i y_i=U_iU_i^{\mathsf T}\nabla f_i(\alpha_i)\), using \(\sum_i r_i\) stored scalars.

notation.meaning: fixed orthonormal sketch basis for component i

review_flags: The supplied locators do not identify this specific estimator-storage representation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinate-storage and orthogonal-projection identities are internally correct and representation is the appropriate knowledge kind, but the specific estimator-storage construction and storage count have no cited source.

A finite-sum objective interface represents \(F:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R\) as \[F(x)= rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x),\] where each component \(f_i:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R\) is differentiable. A component oracle accepts \((x,i)\) and returns \((f_i(x),

knowledge_statements.title: Empirical-Risk Objective Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample-average loss interface for supervised empirical-risk minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given observations \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathcal Z\), a parameter set \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and a loss \(\ell:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R\), the empirical-risk objective is \[\widehat R_n(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(x;z_i),\qquad x\in\mathcal X.\] Its sample oracle returns \(\ell(x;z_i)\) and, when differentiable in \(x\), \(\nabla_x\ell(x;z_i)\). Thus empirical-risk minimization is the finite-sum problem \(\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\widehat R_n(x)\), possibly with \(\mathcal X\) encoding inductive bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Empirical risk averages the loss over observed samples and exposes each sample loss, and optionally its gradient, as a finite-sum component oracle.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell(x;z_i)\) is finite on \(\mathcal X\); gradient output requires differentiability in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\widehat R_n(x)=\min_{x\in\mathcal X}n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(x;z_i)\).

children.title: Product-Set Constraints
children.top_down_role: Subspace interfaces for feasible regions expressed through product-set structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Set Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cartesian-product constraints aligned with a fixed finite-dimensional block decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(d_j\in\mathbb N\), and let \(X_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_j}\) be nonempty for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). Their product-set constraint is \[X=\prod_{j=1}^m X_j=\left\{x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\prod_{j=1}^m\mathbb R^{d_j}:x_j\in X_j\text{ for every }j\right\}.\] Membership in \(X\) is therefore equivalent to simultaneous block membership. If every \(X_j\) is convex, then \(X\) is convex; if every \(X_j\) is closed, then \(X\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite-dimensional block space, a product constraint requires every variable block to belong to its corresponding set. Convexity and closedness pass from all factors to the product.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\), \(d_j\in\mathbb N\), and \(\varnothing\ne X_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_j}\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in X\Longleftrightarrow x_j\in X_j\) for every \(j\).

notation.meaning: feasible set in the j-th Euclidean block space

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Separable Constraint Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint sets whose feasibility separates across a fixed decomposition into variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty block sets \(X_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_j}\), let \(X=\prod_{j=1}^m X_j\). The set \(X\) is block-separable with respect to this decomposition because \(x\in X\) holds exactly when \(x_j\in X_j\) for every \(j\). Equivalently, with the extended-real indicator \(\delta_C(u)=0\) for \(u\in C\) and \(\delta_C(u)=+\infty\) otherwise, \[\delta_X(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m\delta_{X_j}(x_j).\] Conversely, the finite-valued locus of the sum on the right is exactly \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint set is block-separable when global feasibility is exactly the conjunction of independent block constraints; equivalently, its indicator is the sum of the block indicators.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\), \(d_j\in\mathbb N\), and \(\varnothing\ne X_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_j}\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in X\Longleftrightarrow (\forall j)\,x_j\in X_j\), equivalently \(\delta_X(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m\delta_{X_j}(x_j)\).

children.title: Blockwise Feasibility Interfaces

knowledge_statements.title: Blockwise Feasibility Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local membership and projection operations implementing product-set feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\prod_{j=1}^m X_j\subseteq\prod_j\mathbb R^{d_j}\), where every \(X_j\) is nonempty, closed, and convex. A blockwise feasibility interface provides membership tests for each \(X_j\) and Euclidean projections \(P_{X_j}\). Global feasibility and projection then decompose as \[x\in X\Longleftrightarrow (\forall j)\ x_j\in X_j,\qquad P_X(x)=\bigl(P_{X_1}(x_1),\ldots,P_{X_m}(x_m)\bigr).\] Hence modifying one block can be made feasible by projecting only that block while leaving already feasible unmodified blocks unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For closed convex product constraints, membership is checked block by block and the global Euclidean projection is the tuple of independent block projections.
assumptions_latex: \(X_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_j}\) is nonempty, closed, and convex for every \(j\).
The product space carries the standard squared Euclidean norm \(\sum_j\lVert x_j\rVert_2^2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Atomic Constraint Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauge-bounded constraints generated by a prescribed family of atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, compact, and contain no zero requirement. Its atomic gauge is \[\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{k=1}^q c_k:x=\sum_{k=1}^q c_k a_k,\ c_k\ge0,\ a_k\in\mathcal A,\ q\in\mathbb N\right\}.\] For \(\tau\ge0\), the associated atomic constraint set is \(C_\tau=\{x:\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)\le\tau\}\). When \(\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\) is closed and contains \(0\), this set equals \(\tau\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atomic constraint bounds the minimum total nonnegative weight needed to express a point as a finite combination of prescribed atoms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_\tau=\{x:\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)\le\tau\}\), and under the stated closure condition \(C_\tau=\tau\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\).

notation.meaning: atomic gauge generated by the atoms
atomic gauge constraint set of radius tau

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Constraint Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex matrix constraints defined by an upper bound on rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(m,n\ge1\) and \(0\le r\le\min\{m,n\}\), the rank-constrained matrix set is \[\mathcal R_r=\{X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}(X)\le r\}.\] Equivalently, \(X\in\mathcal R_r\) exactly when there exist \(U\in\mathbb R^{m\times r}\) and \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\) such that \(X=UV^{\mathsf T}\). The set \(\mathcal R_r\) is closed; it is nonconvex whenever \(0<r<\min\{m,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is feasible when its rank is at most the prescribed bound, equivalently when it admits a factorization through that many latent dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\mathcal R_r\Longleftrightarrow (\exists U,V)\ X=UV^{\mathsf T}\) with \(r\) factor columns.

notation.meaning: set of matrices of rank at most r

review_flags: No supplied locator directly treats low-rank constraint sets and their factorization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-bounded set, factorization equivalence, closedness, and stated nonconvex regime are mathematically standard and fit a definition container, but none has a supplied source locator.

children.title: Atom-Rank Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Navigation for cases where atomic representations induce or approximate low-rank structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Atom-Rank Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-one atomic decompositions and their relation to matrix rank and nuclear norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A=\{uv^{\mathsf T}:u\in\mathbb R^m,\ v\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert u\rVert_2=\lVert v\rVert_2=1\}\). A matrix \(X\) has rank at most \(r\) if and only if it can be written as \[X=\sum_{k=1}^r c_k A_k,\qquad c_k\ge0,\quad A_k\in\mathcal A,\] allowing zero coefficients. Moreover, the atomic gauge generated by \(\mathcal A\) equals the nuclear norm: \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}(X)=\lVert X\rVert_*\). Thus rank counts the minimum number of rank-one atoms, whereas the nuclear norm measures their minimum total weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix rank is the fewest unit rank-one atoms needed in a weighted decomposition, while the corresponding atomic gauge is the nuclear norm.
assumptions_latex: Atoms include both signs because \(u\) and \(-u\) are both admissible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\le r\Longleftrightarrow X=\sum_{k=1}^r c_kA_k\), and \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}(X)=\lVert X\rVert_*\).

notation.meaning: atomic gauge of the rank-one atoms
nuclear norm, the sum of singular values

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The SVD-based rank-one atomic decomposition and nuclear-norm gauge identity are mathematically consistent and representation is the correct role, but the nontrivial correspondence has no cited source.

children.title: Affine Constraint Sets
children.top_down_role: Subspace interfaces for feasible regions specified by affine restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Constraint Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine sets presented by linear equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\). The affine constraint set determined by \((A,b)\) is \[\mathcal{C}(A,b):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:Ax=b\}.\] If \(\mathcal{C}(A,b)\neq\varnothing\), then for every \(x_0\in\mathcal{C}(A,b)\), \[\mathcal{C}(A,b)=x_0+\ker(A).\] Thus a nonempty equality-constrained feasible region is a translate of the linear subspace \(\ker(A)\); the empty set is permitted when the equations are inconsistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solutions of Ax=b form either an empty set or a translate of the null space of A by any particular solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{C}(A,b)=\{x:Ax=b\}\), and if \(x_0\in\mathcal{C}(A,b)\), then \(\mathcal{C}(A,b)=x_0+\ker(A)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Equation Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact consistency criterion for a finite-dimensional linear-equation interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), the equation \(Ax=b\) is feasible exactly when \(b\in\operatorname{range}(A)\). Equivalently, \[Ax=b\text{ has a solution}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y^{\mathsf T}b=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker(A^{\mathsf T}).\] Hence feasibility can be certified by a particular solution, while infeasibility can be certified by a vector \(y\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(y^{\mathsf T}b\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ax=b is feasible exactly when b lies in the range of A, equivalently when b is orthogonal to every vector in the left null space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x\; Ax=b\iff b\in\operatorname{range}(A)\iff b\perp\ker(A^{\mathsf T})\).

children.title: Null-Space Parameterization
children.top_down_role: Use of null-space coordinates to expose feasible subspace directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Null-Space Parameterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-coordinate representation of a consistent affine equality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\). Suppose \(Ax=b\) is feasible, choose \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(Ax_0=b\), and let \(N\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\) have columns forming a basis of \(\ker(A)\), where \(r=n-\operatorname{rank}(A)\). Then \[\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:Ax=b\}=\{x_0+Nz:z\in\mathbb{R}^{r}\}.\] Because \(N\) has full column rank, the parameter \(z\) is unique. Consequently, for any objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(Ax=b\) is equivalent, under the bijection \(x=x_0+Nz\), to unconstrained minimization of \(z\mapsto f(x_0+Nz)\) over \(\mathbb{R}^r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every feasible point equals one particular solution plus a unique null-space basis combination. This bijection converts optimization over the equality-constrained set into unconstrained optimization in the reduced coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b\}=\{x_0+Nz:z\in\mathbb{R}^{r}\}\), with a unique \(z\) for each feasible \(x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Forward-Mode Automatic Differentiation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-mode acquisition of gradient projections for a scalar differentiable objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable at \(x\), and let \(S=[s_1,\ldots,s_k]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\). Forward-mode automatic differentiation propagates each tangent direction \(s_j\) through a computational program for \(f\) and returns the directional derivatives \(D f(x)[s_j]\). For a scalar objective, their vector representation is \[\bigl(D f(x)[s_1],\ldots,D f(x)[s_k]\bigr)^{\mathsf T}=S^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(x).\] Thus forward mode obtains a sketched or subspace-projected gradient without first materializing the full gradient vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward-mode differentiation propagates chosen tangent directions and returns their inner products with the gradient, directly producing a projected gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D f(x)[S]=S^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(x)\), interpreted columnwise in the seed directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Undersized Sketches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension barrier for embedding a fixed subspace by a linear sketch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) have orthonormal columns and let \(S\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be any linear sketch. If \(m<d\), then \(SU\) has a nontrivial null space: there exists \(z\neq0\) such that \(SUz=0\). Consequently, no \(\varepsilon\)-subspace embedding inequality \[(1-\varepsilon)\lVert Uz\rVert_2^2\leq\lVert SUz\rVert_2^2\leq(1+\varepsilon)\lVert Uz\rVert_2^2\] can hold for every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) when \(0\leq\varepsilon<1\). This obstruction is deterministic and cannot be removed by changing the sketch distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sketch with fewer rows than the subspace dimension necessarily annihilates a nonzero subspace vector, so it cannot be a relative-error embedding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker(SU)\neq\{0\}\), so no \(\varepsilon\)-embedding with \(\varepsilon<1\) exists on \(\operatorname{range}(U)\).

notation.meaning: Orthonormal basis of the target subspace

children.title: High-Coherence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where concentrated geometric influence undermines nominal sketch behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Coherence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform row sampling can miss directions concentrated on a few coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) have orthonormal columns, with leverage scores \(\ell_i=\lVert e_i^{\mathsf T}U\rVert_2^2\) and coherence \(\mu=(n/d)\max_i\ell_i\). In the maximally coherent example \(U=[e_1,\ldots,e_d]\), one has \(\mu=n/d\). If \(m\) rows are sampled independently and uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), then any fixed active coordinate \(i\leq d\) is omitted with probability \((1-1/n)^m\). On that event the sampled matrix annihilates \(e_i\), so it cannot embed \(\operatorname{range}(U)\) with distortion below one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a coordinate-aligned high-coherence subspace, uniform sampling can omit an active coordinate and completely lose its direction.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) row indices are sampled independently and uniformly
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(i\leq d\), omission occurs with probability \((1-1/n)^m\) and causes embedding failure.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit coordinate-subspace calculation and elementary sampling probability
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinate-subspace example, coherence value, and row-omission probability are mathematically consistent and fit the failure-boundary leaf. No cited source supports the coherence and sampling-failure formulation.

children.title: Sampling-Distribution Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by disagreement between the sampling law and the problem's influential directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-Distribution Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by assigning too little probability to a high-leverage row.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) have orthonormal columns, and sample \(m\) row indices independently from probabilities \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\). If a row \(i\) has leverage score \(\ell_i>0\), then it is never observed with probability \((1-p_i)^m\). In particular, if \(p_i=0\), every sampled-and-rescaled sketch annihilates the component of the subspace visible only through row \(i\). More generally, for the coordinate subspace containing \(e_i\), omission of row \(i\) makes any relative-error embedding inequality with distortion \(\varepsilon<1\) fail on that direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the sampling distribution underweights a row needed by the target subspace, that row may be missed and its associated direction lost entirely.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) row samples are independent with probabilities \((p_i)_{i=1}^{n}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The row-omission probability is \((1-p_i)^m\); for a uniquely supported direction, omission forces embedding failure.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact independent-sampling omission probability applied to a coordinate-supported subspace
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact omission probability is correct, and the embedding-failure conclusion is properly restricted to a direction uniquely supported on the omitted row. An inspectable source is still required for this sampling-mismatch failure statement.

children.title: Leverage-Blind Sampling
children.top_down_role: Sampling failures associated with ignoring strongly nonuniform leverage structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Leverage-Blind Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional counterexample to uniform sampling without leverage information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(n\geq2\) and take the one-dimensional subspace basis \(U=e_1\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times1}\). Form a row-sampling sketch from \(m\) independent uniform coordinate samples, with any finite rescaling of sampled rows. With probability \[(1-1/n)^m,\] coordinate \(1\) is never sampled. On this event \(SU=0\), although \(\lVert U\rVert_2=1\). Therefore leverage-blind uniform sampling fails every \(\varepsilon\)-subspace embedding condition with \(\varepsilon<1\) on this instance. To make this failure probability at most \(\delta\), it is necessary that \(m\geq\log(1/\delta)/[-\log(1-1/n)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform coordinate sampling misses a subspace concentrated on one coordinate with probability (1−1/n)^m, producing total loss of that direction.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) coordinates are sampled independently and uniformly
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(SU=0)=(1-1/n)^m\), implying \(m\geq\log(1/\delta)/[-\log(1-1/n)]\) for failure probability at most \(\delta\).

children.title: Single-Trial Tail Risk
children.top_down_role: Rare but consequential sketch or subspace outcomes within an individual trial.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Trial Tail Risk
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual possible failure probability of one randomized sketch or subspace draw.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a randomized sketch and let \(E\) denote the event that \(S\) satisfies the accuracy condition required by one projected first-order update, such as a prescribed subspace-embedding inequality. If \(\Pr(E)\geq1-\delta\), where \(0\leq\delta\leq1\), then \[\Pr(E^{\mathsf c})\leq\delta.\] A conclusion proved only under the condition \(E\) does not, by itself, apply on \(E^{\mathsf c}\). Thus, without a deterministic safeguard or a separately verified certificate, the analysis leaves a possible single-trial bad event whose probability is bounded above by \(\delta\); the bound \(\delta>0\) does not imply that the actual bad-event probability is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-shot sketch guarantee bounds the possible bad-event probability by delta, but a conclusion conditioned on successful sketching does not cover that bad event. A positive upper bound does not imply that failures actually occur with positive probability.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is the event required by the update analysis
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(E^{\mathsf c})\leq\delta\), and guarantees conditioned on \(E\) do not by themselves cover \(E^{\mathsf c}\).

notation.meaning: Upper bound on the single-trial failure probability

children.title: Failure Accumulation
children.top_down_role: Compounding risk across repeated sketches, iterations, or adaptive queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Accumulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon aggregation of per-iteration sketch failure probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(T\geq1\). For randomized iterations \(t=1,\ldots,T\), let \(F_t\) be the event that the sketch used at iteration \(t\) fails its required condition, and suppose \(\Pr(F_t)\leq\delta_t\). Without any independence assumption, \[\Pr\!\left(\bigcup_{t=1}^{T}F_t\right)\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_t.\] If the events \(F_1,\ldots,F_T\) are mutually independent and \(\Pr(F_t)=\delta_t\) for every \(t\), then \[\Pr\!\left(\bigcup_{t=1}^{T}F_t\right)=1-\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1-\delta_t).\] Hence a horizon-wide reliability target requires controlling the aggregate of the per-iteration failure probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over a finite horizon, the probability of at least one sketch failure is bounded by the sum of the per-step failure bounds. For mutually independent events with the stated probabilities, it equals one minus the product of their success probabilities.
assumptions_latex: \(F_t\) is the failure event at iteration \(t\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(\bigcup_{t=1}^{T}F_t)\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_t\); under mutual independence and \(\Pr(F_t)=\delta_t\), it equals \(1-\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1-\delta_t)\).

notation.meaning: Positive finite number of randomized iterations

children.title: Restart Vulnerability
children.top_down_role: Regimes where retries or restarts do not adequately control repeated failure exposure.

knowledge_statements.title: Restart Vulnerability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure probability under repeated restarts with reused or independently resampled sketches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a sketched method fail on an event \(F(S)\) having probability \(p>0\). If every restart reuses the same sketch \(S\), then for any number \(r\ge 1\) of restarts, the probability that all runs fail remains \(p\), not \(p^r\). If sketches \(S_1,\ldots,S_r\) are independent and each run fails exactly on \(F(S_i)\), then the all-failure probability is \(p^r\), while the probability of at least one failure is \(1-(1-p)^r\). Thus restart guarantees require an explicit independence convention and a success-based aggregation rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reusing one bad sketch makes every restart fail together; independent resampling only helps when outputs are aggregated by accepting at least one successful run.
assumptions_latex: \(S_1,\ldots,S_r\) are independent in the resampled regime.
Each single-run failure event has probability \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\Pr(\text{all fail under reuse})=p,\qquad \Pr(\text{all fail independently})=p^r.\]

notation.meaning: failure event determined by sketch S

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Query Breakdown
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed-query embedding guarantee need not cover queries selected after observing the sketch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^k\) be a realized linear sketch with \(k<n\). A guarantee proved for a fixed query \(g\), independent of \(S\), does not imply the same guarantee for an adaptive query \(g(S)\). Indeed, choose a measurable unit vector \(g(S)\in\ker S\) whenever \(S\) has rank \(k\). Then \(\|g(S)\|_2=1\) but \(\|Sg(S)\|_2=0\). Hence any lower norm-preservation bound \(\|Sg\|_2\ge c\|g\|_2\) with \(c>0\) fails for this adaptive query.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive query can select a unit vector in the realized sketch kernel, defeating norm preservation even when every fixed query is protected with high probability.
assumptions_latex: The query may depend measurably on the realized sketch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\|g(S)\|_2=1\quad\text{and}\quad \|Sg(S)\|_2=0.\]

notation.meaning: realized linear sketch from R^n to R^k

abla f(x)=0\), then \(\langle
abla f(x),dangle=0\) for every \(d\in U\). Consequently, no direction available to a method restricted to \(U\) is a strict first-order descent direction at \(x\), even when \(
abla f(x)
e0\). For the linear objective \(f(z)=\langle g,zangle\), any nonzero \(g\in U^\perp\) realizes this failure exactly.

knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Blind Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directions omitted by every sampled space remain invisible to all restricted first-order steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((U_t)_{t\ge0}\) be sampled search subspaces of \(\mathbb R^n\), and suppose a nonzero vector \(v\) satisfies \(v\in\bigcap_{t\ge0}U_t^\perp\). If an algorithm generates \(x_{t+1}-x_t\in U_t\), then \(\langle v,x_t\rangle=\langle v,x_0\rangle\) for every \(t\). Therefore the algorithm cannot alter the component of its iterate along \(v\). In particular, for \(f(x)=\tfrac12(\langle v,x\rangle-b)^2\), any initialization with \(\langle v,x_0\rangle\ne b\) retains a positive objective residual forever.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\langle v,x_t\rangle=\langle v,x_0\rangle\quad\text{for every }t\ge0.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Biased Projected Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncorrected random projection need not provide an unbiased full-gradient estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=\nabla f(x)\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(S\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) be random, and form the lifted projected quantity \(\widehat g=SS^\top g\). Its expectation is \(\mathbb E[\widehat g]=\mathbb E[SS^\top]g\). Hence \(\widehat g\) is unbiased for every possible gradient \(g\) if and only if \(\mathbb E[SS^\top]=I_n\). If this isotropy identity fails, any \(g\) outside the nullspace of \(\mathbb E[SS^\top]-I_n\) has nonzero bias, so an analysis treating \(\widehat g\) as an unbiased full gradient is invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted projected gradient is unbiased for all gradients exactly when the sketch covariance is the identity; otherwise systematic directional bias remains.
assumptions_latex: The gradient \(g\) is fixed independently of the current sketch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathbb E[\widehat g]=g\text{ for all }g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathbb E[SS^\top]=I_n.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Incompatible Composite Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A restricted proximal subproblem may be infeasible or differ essentially from the full proximal step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a composite objective \(F=f+h\), where \(h=\delta_C\) is the indicator of a nonempty closed convex set \(C\). A subspace method restricted to the affine space \(x+U\) requires projection onto \(C\cap(x+U)\), not merely projection onto \(C\). This restricted proximal map can be undefined even though the full proximal map exists. In \(\mathbb R^2\), take \(C=\{z:z_2=0\}\), \(x=(0,1)\), and \(U=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)\}\). Then \(C\cap(x+U)=\varnothing\), whereas \(\operatorname{prox}_{h}(x)=P_Cx=(0,0)\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C\cap(x+U)=\varnothing\quad\text{while}\quad \operatorname{prox}_{\delta_C}(x)=P_Cx\text{ exists}.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Sketch-Cost Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sketch construction can erase arithmetic savings from a lower-dimensional update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a full-space iteration costs \(C_{\mathrm{full}}\), while a sketched iteration costs \(C_{\mathrm{sketch}}+C_{\mathrm{sub}}\), including sketch formation or application and the subspace update. If the full and sketched methods require respectively \(T_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon)\) and \(T_{\mathrm{sk}}(\varepsilon)\) iterations to produce the same \(\varepsilon\)-certificate, then sketching gives no operation-count improvement whenever \(T_{\mathrm{sk}}(\varepsilon)(C_{\mathrm{sketch}}+C_{\mathrm{sub}})\ge T_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon)C_{\mathrm{full}}\). In particular, per-iteration dominance \(C_{\mathrm{sketch}}+C_{\mathrm{sub}}\ge C_{\mathrm{full}}\), together with \(T_{\mathrm{sk}}(\varepsilon)\ge T_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon)\), precludes improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sketching cannot reduce total work when sketch formation plus the reduced update costs at least as much overall as the full-space method.
assumptions_latex: Both methods use the same operation-count model.
Both iteration counts refer to the same accuracy certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_{\mathrm{sk}}(\varepsilon)(C_{\mathrm{sketch}}+C_{\mathrm{sub}})\ge T_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon)C_{\mathrm{full}}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{no total-work improvement}.\]

notation.meaning: cost of constructing or applying one sketch

knowledge_statements.title: Iteration Inflation from Small Subspaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform coordinate-subspace updates exhibit an explicit dimension-to-sketch-size iteration penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), let each iteration choose uniformly a subset \(I_t\) of \(k\) coordinates and exactly minimize over their span, thereby setting the selected coordinates to zero. Conditional on \(x_t\), each coordinate survives with probability \(1-k/n\), so \(\mathbb E[\|x_{t+1}\|_2^2\mid x_t]=(1-k/n)\|x_t\|_2^2\). Consequently, \(\mathbb E[f(x_T)]=(1-k/n)^T f(x_0)\), and achieving \(\mathbb E[f(x_T)]\le\varepsilon f(x_0)\) requires \(T\ge \log(1/\varepsilon)/[-\log(1-k/n)]\), which is asymptotic to \((n/k)\log(1/\varepsilon)\) when \(k/n\) is small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Updating only k uniformly sampled coordinates contracts this quadratic by 1−k/n per iteration, producing an approximately n/k iteration inflation.
assumptions_latex: \(1\le k<n\), and coordinate subsets are sampled uniformly.
Selected coordinates are minimized exactly at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathbb E[f(x_T)]=\left(1-\frac{k}{n}\right)^T f(x_0),\qquad T\ge\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{-\log(1-k/n)}.\]

notation.meaning: uniformly sampled set of k coordinates

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Space Certificate-Cost Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost boundary when every sketched iteration requires a full-dimensional stopping certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a sketched method perform \(N_s(\varepsilon)\) iterations, each costing \(C_s(n,r)\) for a rank-\(r\) update and \(C_{mathrm{cert}}(n)\) for a full-space certificate. Its work is \(W_s(\varepsilon)=N_s(\varepsilon)(C_s(n,r)+C_{mathrm{cert}}(n))\). Let a full-space method have work \(W_f(\varepsilon)=N_f(\varepsilon)C_f(n)\). If \(C_{mathrm{cert}}(n)\ge C_f(n)\) and \(N_s(\varepsilon)\ge N_f(\varepsilon)\), then \(W_s(\varepsilon)\ge W_f(\varepsilon)\), irrespective of the reduced update cost. Thus a mandatory full-space certificate eliminates any worst-case work advantage unless certification is amortized or the sketched method reduces the iteration count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-space certificate costing at least one baseline iteration prevents a work improvement whenever sketching does not reduce the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: Both methods use the same accuracy criterion \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[W_s(\varepsilon)\ge W_f(\varepsilon).\]

total work of the sketched and full-space methods

knowledge_statements.title: Absence of Intrinsic-Dimension Advantage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isotropic quadratic example showing cancellation between cheaper subspace steps and iteration inflation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert x\rVert_2^2\) for \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). At iteration \(k\), independently draw a Haar-uniform rank-\(r\) orthogonal projector \(P_k\) and set \(x_{k+1}=(I-P_k)x_k\). Then \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert x_{k+1}\rVert_2^2\mid x_k]=(1-r/n)\lVert x_k\rVert_2^2\), and hence \(\mathbb{E}\lVert x_k\rVert_2^2=(1-r/n)^k\lVert x_0\rVert_2^2\). For fixed \(r/n\) bounded away from \(1\), attaining \(\mathbb{E}\lVert x_k\rVert_2^2\le \varepsilon\lVert x_0\rVert_2^2\) requires \(k=\Theta((n/r)\log(1/\varepsilon))\). If an iteration uses \(\Theta(r)\) directional operations, the total directional work is \(\Theta(n\log(1/\varepsilon))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the isotropic quadratic, independent rank-r random projections reduce expected squared error by a factor of 1-r/n per iteration. When r/n stays bounded away from one, the factor-r reduction in per-step directional work is canceled by reciprocal iteration inflation.
assumptions_latex: The projectors \(P_k\) are independent and Haar-uniform among rank-\(r\) orthogonal projectors.
For the stated \(\Theta\)-estimate, \(r/n\) is bounded above by a constant strictly smaller than \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[k=\Theta\!\left(\frac{n}{r}\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right),\qquad rk=\Theta\!\left(n\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right).\]
